claims.text: The target nanoparticles contain five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios.
The as-synthesized nanoparticles are homogeneous solid solutions.
Maintenance of structural and chemical stability from 473 to 1923 K is governed by the development and persistence of local chemical ordering.
Local chemical ordering increases the ruggedness of the energy landscape.
Local chemical ordering increases activation barriers for atomic diffusion.
Increased energy-landscape ruggedness produces sluggish atomic diffusion.
Chemically disordered concentrated solid solutions are often metastable because of enthalpic interactions.
Element-specific interactions create locally enhanced binding regions that constitute local chemical order.
Local chemical ordering slows atomic rearrangements and delays or prevents elemental segregation.
Local-chemical-order-mediated kinetic barriers preserve a metastable single-phase structure and chemical homogeneity during catalytic or thermoelectric operation.
Nanoparticles with robust local chemical order will retain a single-phase solid-solution structure with minimal segregation or phase transitions throughout 473–1923 K.
Retention of robust local chemical order will result in stable catalytic or thermoelectric properties over the operating-temperature range.
Weak or disrupted local chemical order will lead to phase separation or chemical inhomogeneity.
Weak or disrupted local chemical order will alter catalytic or thermoelectric performance.
The mechanism should hold when temperature is the primary variable and additional chemical agents do not promote segregation or secondary-phase formation.
Rapid quenching or excessive chemical interactions can override the intrinsic sluggish diffusion attributed to local chemical order.
Above an unspecified temperature threshold, local chemical order can no longer counteract thermally activated diffusion.
The controlled comparison is between nanoparticles ramped through 473–1923 K under operating conditions and nanoparticles maintained at room temperature.
The quantitative relationship between local chemical order and temperature-dependent diffusion activation energy is not established and may vary by elemental combination.
Segregation, chemical inhomogeneity, and functional degradation after heating despite initial local-order signatures would falsify the hypothesis.
